title: Jack Laine's drummers, wire brushes and Schellang
summary: Sal says he introduced wire brushes, compares himself to earlier drummers, and tells of fights with August Schellinger.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: What did you talk to, Benny?

The Jack Lapine, Abbie, had a sweet-tone of the trumpet. And it was playing up there, open-air, see. And the other day, they didn't have them up for the trumpet. Had to put a pillow in. The boy says, I hear you. You get fired. I said, well, with wire brushes. Why brushes? We're just picking the kind of problem at the time, see. Well, that was right down the alley. Because they had guys before my time, they could make a good roll, and I could, see. But I was a little more modern, see. I had to put the socks up. I could play four beats. I pushed them back. It was better than they could, see. But I was a little more advanced, see. Like the guys today, they're real advanced now. I'm playing my band. Man, I said, what the hell you got there, man? He said, the water brushes, man. Never heard of wire brush. I thought, I don't like that, you know. Fend, snare drum. Tight snare, you know. Little dancing drum, man. But a French drum. Sharp sound, see. Now, when the guy goes, I could go to the rock. I could do that, man. Or I could play the other thing, see. So, after getting jobs, you see. Things began to change, you see. Emmett Wright, which was a fine drummer. He bought a saxophone. But he couldn't play it, see. So I bought it cheap, see. As good a drummer as he was, see. He didn't have the coordination, see. To play four beats, see, in two years, see. Or to play a different hand, different upper. Well, I always could do that, man. I don't know why. He said, nah, man. I could always play one thing here, one over here, and the different over here. I was good, see. Even when I started, so I was at the same room, see. When I had a job, man, up at the team in the club, but I never had to go to work there. They raised my pleasure. So I go up there one night, and everybody drunk up there. I see a guy, an ex-boyfriend of Ampat Gilk, and they can reach out bootleg and a tough guy. So, he took a room one night. He was beating my head on the table. I picked my head, boom, boom, boom, on the table. I said, Jesus, God. And man, and then Shalang and I always got in a fight, see. Shalang, man. I was going to take his plate, see. And at that time, I thought Shalang was a digger. He was a drummer, Shalang, see. But I thought it was a digger. I don't know why. And I wanted a digger, a friend of mine. Fred Lloyd Cannon, see. Fred and I was with him, Joe, you know. I said, I like the digger, man. He said, Bluffer, man. So, I said to the guy, Shalang, man. I said, I'll take you on. I said, you want to fight? Let's go outside. He talked plenty big, see. He wouldn't go outside. He got small one night with Abbie, man. Abbie was a good piece of man, see. And he slapped the hell out of him. Abbie Brunas, man. Abbie was a nice guy, see. He didn't take the food, I said. But Shalang, he died like the old dad with a bull in his head. He died, somebody shot. Yeah, a mysterious death. You know what I'll tell you. Shalang got a job, he was a good promoter, and I thought, I don't know, for some reason, I thought back in the olden days, I thought Shalang was a good drummer. I did. He had a good beat, man. He played with it from his heart, man. I like it all. That man, he had the job bouncing, a henchman in Chicago, in a group and all, multi-hills and whatever. So, I said, he's a barber, see. He takes to cut my hair from down the street, see. All he had to cut on his hair, see. He was a good guy, dressed good, you know. The gangster type, you know. And I can say again, I thought he was a good drummer too. So, man, I met him one day, I said, I said, I ain't talked to you. What did you say, your mother rule? I said, talk, you know. I said, what you doing, you barking? He said, no, man. I'm a chauffeur for, for Chet Morris, and driving a big car, you see. Then he got a job deputy on St. George's. He said, give me a highball. The guy said, the joint's closed. The guy said, I said, give me one, man. The joint's closed. The gun out, started shooting the place. That's the kind of guy he was. Then, the far line, he, he'd be out on some of the push. You know. He did what? In other words, he kind of worked with that PR, see. As who put, the man in the mood, you know. Yeah. Even though he smoked it, see. He had to leave town, he was gone for about ten years. He was about ten years.
